extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (researchers and advanced students); historians of mathematics; readers interested in standards for mathematical problems and proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards (from Hilbert's 1900 address) for what makes a good mathematical problem and what constitutes an acceptable/valuable solution or proof, including clarity, difficulty, rigour, applicability, and methodological consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness and ease of comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical problem should have 'clearness and ease of comprehension' — more so than a theory; what is clear and easily comprehended attracts while the complicated repels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert emphasizes that a perfect problem is one that can be stated simply and understood readily. Example quote: 'This clearness and ease of comprehension ... I should still more demand for a mathematical problem if it is to be perfect.' Anti-pattern: overly convoluted or obscure problem statements that deter interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate level of difficulty (enticing but accessible)
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem should be difficult enough to entice and test investigators, yet not completely inaccessible so as not to mock our efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert frames difficulty as a motivator: problems must entice the community without being hopeless. Good problems serve as 'guide posts' and provide pleasure when solved. Anti-pattern: problems either trivial or provably unreachable given current methods/hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance / deep significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems should have deep significance for the advance of mathematical science in general and play an important role in the work of individual investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert notes that problems which influence development broadly or unlock multiple areas are especially valuable (examples: Fermat's Last Theorem, three-body problem). Scoring note: value is judged by the gain science obtains from their solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility in generating new methods and outlooks
rubrics_metrics.description: A good problem should lead to the discovery of new methods, new outlooks, and broaden the investigator's horizon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert gives historical examples where pursuing a problem (e.g., Bernoulli’s brachistochrone, Fermat's problem) led to entire new theories (calculus of variations, ideal numbers). A desirable criterion is that solving or attempting the problem produces tools useful elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact formulation of hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypotheses implied in the statement of the problem must always be exactly formulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert insists on precise problem statements so solutions rest on clearly stated assumptions. Anti-pattern: vague or implicit hypotheses that hide essential conditions and prevent finite-step verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provability by a finite number of logical steps (rigour)
rubrics_metrics.description: A solution shall be possible to establish correct by means of a finite number of steps based upon a finite number of hypotheses — i.e., rigour in reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a core requirement: proofs must be finitely checkable and grounded in explicit hypotheses. Hilbert links this requirement to the philosophical necessity of rigour and to the full effect and suggestiveness of a problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigour fosters simplicity and development
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigour is not the enemy of simplicity; rather, rigorous methods frequently lead to simpler, more comprehensible, and more developable approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert gives examples where imposing rigour simplified theory (algebraic curves, power series, calculus of variations via Weierstrass). Scoring guidance: favour proofs that, while rigorous, also simplify or unify theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic grounding for new concepts and geometric signs
rubrics_metrics.description: New concepts and geometric signs must be investigated axiomatically so their conceptual content is rigorously known before using geometric diagrams in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert argues that geometric figures are mnemonic signs but their use as strict proof requires mastery of underlying axioms. Anti-pattern: relying on geometric intuition without axiomatic justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice and clarity of notation/signs
rubrics_metrics.description: New signs (notations) should be chosen to remind us of the phenomena that motivated the concepts and to aid understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert treats arithmetical symbols and geometric figures as 'written diagrams' that facilitate reasoning. Guidance: prefer notation that is mnemonic and clarifying rather than obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relating special problems to more general standpoints (generality/method formation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure often comes from not recognizing a more general standpoint; reframing a special problem as part of a chain of related problems can yield general methods applicable to many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cauchy's complex paths, Kummer's ideals. Methodological guidance: seek the general setting that subsumes the problem to obtain broader tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specialization and solving simpler subproblems
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialization (solving simpler or related subproblems) is often more important than generalization for overcoming difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert advises finding easier problems and solving them with devices as perfect as possible; this frequently yields concepts capable of generalization. Anti-pattern: attempting over-general approaches before resolving simpler cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving impossibility when appropriate (negative results count)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solution cannot be achieved under given hypotheses, one should show the impossibility of the solution; proofs of impossibility are legitimate and valuable outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert cites classical examples (irrationality proofs, impossibility of squaring the circle under original intent) and notes that impossibility proofs can settle problems usefully and lead to deeper principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay of pure and applied sources (fertility from both experience and reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems may originate from external experience (applied needs) or pure reason (internal development); both sources are important and their interplay leads to fruitful analogies and new questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert stresses that applied problems open new branches and that internal logical combinations produce deep pure problems (e.g., number theory). Good problems often connect or transfer methods between branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of solvability (conviction that problems admit exact settlement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert articulates a philosophical axiom: every definite mathematical problem ought to be susceptible of an exact settlement, either by an actual answer or by proof of impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conviction motivates work: mathematicians should seek finite logical resolutions. While Hilbert notes it as a conviction rather than a proven theorem, it functions as an evaluative standard and an incentive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness across branches (cross-applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable problem is one whose solution or study finds application in diverse and seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert gives examples where single problems (shortest line, regular polyhedra) impacted geometry, group theory, differential equations, mechanics, etc. Scoring note: higher value if a problem unlocks multiple areas.
